A new method for classifying blazars observed by the Fermi Gamma-ray Telescope is presented, employing a Bayesian artificial neural network approach. Data from the Fermi LAT 3rd Catalogue in the region $|b| \le 20^\circ$ was utilized to differentiate between SPideR (Sparse, Point-like, or Extended) types. The nomenclature "SPideR" refers to previous classification methods. A detailed analysis compared classification outcomes across various network configurations and training-validation-testing sets. The results showed that classification accuracy was influenced by both the selected parameters and the test data. The study identified challenging sources, mainly sparse or unresolved blazars with high or low gamma-ray fluxes, which were difficult to classify. The sources' spectral energy distributions were found to correlate with classification accuracy. The proposed method is adaptable to other astrophysical classification problems involving multi-dimensional datasets.

Automating social media content creation can enhance user experience, 
free time, and productivity. This can be especially beneficial for individuals 
with limited time or seasonal fluctuations in workload. To explore the 
feasibility of automating social media content creation, we conducted a survey 
to gather user perspectives on desired features. The results highlight users' 
apprehensions about automated content creation, including missing human touch, 
lost user engagement, and lost benefits. These concerns can be categorized into 
three themes. We also discovered that user preferences on automated content creation 
are ambiguous, influenced by their personal experiences and situations. Factoring 
in these considerations can aid developers in creating more intuitive interfaces 
and mitigating potential user concerns when implementing automated content creation 
tools.

The tensor product of two hypergraphs, initially introduced for graphs by Bollobás and Nikiforov in 2015, is broadened to hypergraphs, enabling their edge sets to be viewed as vectors within a tensor product space, defined as the least common superspace to the tensor product spaces of the individual hypergraphs. In this study, the spectrum of a hypergraph is defined as the set of eigenvalues of the hypergraph's adjacency tensor, its subgraph spectrum as the set of eigenvalues of the adjacency tensor of a hypergraph's subgraph, and the transitive or simplicial similitude spectrum as the set of eigenvalues of the adjacency tensors of the most general type of transitive or simplicial pairs of hypergraphs. Notably, the transitive or simplicial similitude spectrum can be of infinite size, and the results include generalizations of previous findings by other researchers, along with novel conclusions about the properties of hypergraph spectra.

A collaborative proposal has been submitted for the Indian Astronomy community's participation in the Square Kilometer Array (SKA) Science Observatory. The proposed project, INSIST: Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope, aims to be a major global space-based observatory in the 2020s. INSIST is designed as a modular instrument that can be used alone or in conjunction with the SKA in space to make scientific discoveries. The proposed telescope features an all-sky ultraviolet (UV) survey instrument paired with a large-aperture telescope to collect spatial information. The INSIST ultraviolet (UV) band spectroscopic space telescope is proposed to be a major observatory to study the baryon universe from cosmic structures to star formation and the cosmic voids. The proposed telescope will have a broad wavelength range of 900 to 3700 Angstroms and a high-resolution spectroscopic capability to study the low-mass stars as well as the high-speed space missions to the solar system and the cosmos. The INSIST will also provide the necessary technology to demonstrate and test various space-based ultraviolet (UV) mission concepts. The proposed Indian participation in the INSIST is suggested to be a collaborative effort between the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the Indian astronomical community.

In medical research, particularly in clinical trials, volunteers receive different treatments under close supervision. The goal is to assess each treatment's safety and effectiveness by tracking participants over a prolonged period. In cases where data is regularly collected over a long time span, an interesting phenomenon arises. Typically, measuring subjectivity can introduce noise in data, causing it to fluctuate around a treatment's average value. We will demonstrate that using a natural cubic spline can help determine a treatment's average effect while also accounting for natural variability in data. We will present an integrated mixed-effects model that combines a natural cubic spline with a linear mixed-effect model. This combined approach allows us to compare various degrees of model flexibility in modeling long-term data trends. We will also discuss how our model can be used to analyze treatment differences while accounting for factors like age, disease progression, and treatment interaction.

Discovering the most prevalent transformation pathways of a material is crucial in understanding its properties and behavior, particularly during phase transitions. This is achieved by mapping the material's configuration in multidimensional space over time, with the resulting dynamic trajectories influenced by external factors such as strain rates. This work focuses on identifying the dominant transformation routes of Au and Fe under strain, with the results indicating the need for variable time step molecular dynamics simulations are necessary to capture all the dominant pathways for certain cases. Additionally, the study compares the effectiveness of different optimization methods in identifying the dominant transformation routes.

This research explores growth estimates for smooth solutions to complex Monge-Ampere equations and a specific Hessian equation, both within a strictly pseudoconvex domain within $\Bbb C^N$, involving biholomorphic embeddings. Moreover, it investigates and provides an in-depth analysis for the first non-zero eigenvalue of a Dirichlet eigenvalue problem within $\Bbb C^N$, related to a concave Monge-Ampere equation.

In the context of typed lambda-calculi, we examine the inherent properties of functions that, when applied to any input, yield outputs within the same domain. We find that certain fundamental characteristics - including the presence of certain pairs of functions, abilities to iterate and invert processes, and the existence of a universal function - imply the capability to compute all regular functions. This leads us to a conjecture that any algebraic system allowing the execution of beta-reductions can execute beta-reductions in any order (confluence), and that this conjecture applies to certain lambda-calculi with syntax that is more complex than lambda-calculi with only variable names. We test this conjecture through verification on specific cases where the lambda-calculi with more complex syntax have already proven to be convergent. We also test whether adding partial functions to the domain of lambda-calculi with more complex syntax can still lead to the conclusion that regular functions can be computed.

This work explores the unique characteristics of Ito and Stratonovich integrals when applied to parametric integrands linked to the dynamic flow of conditional probability distributions, with the objective of deriving an equivalent relationship between these integrals that is analogous to the local characteristic formula in stochastic analysis. The research further delves into parameter space calculations, involving the geometric mean of conditional mutual information, to derive a specific formula when the parametric family is determined by a normal distribution.

This note examines the properties that distinguish various group types within the context of topological spaces. It becomes apparent that the topological groups stand out due to their consistent behavior across both compactly generated and Hausdorff spaces. In contrast, this distinct behavior is lost when considering spaces that are either sigma-compact generated or the result of combining a Hausdorff space with a discrete one. As such, the concept of topological groups serves as an exceptional and unique case. To further emphasize this distinction, it is demonstrated that no analogous consistency is exhibited by the categories of semitopological or hypergroupoids when considering similar space configurations.

Natural language is a complex and dynamic form of communication. It is subject to variations in regional dialects, writing styles, and grammatical constructions. Differing linguistic patterns can result in diverse expression of the same intent, posing a challenge to text analysis across domains. To address this issue, we develop a text analysis system capable of interpreting linguistic variations. It incorporates an auxiliary task to improve the system's generalizability on out-of-domain data. We achieve this goal by introducing auxiliary labels to facilitate learning of general linguistic rules. These rules can be transferred to new domains with minimal manual input, thereby enhancing the system's end-to-end performance on out-of-domain data. Our proposed approach is tested on a cross-domain text analysis benchmark, demonstrating improved results and greater generalizability on out-of-domain data.

This paper introduces an information-theoretic framework for safe navigation in collaborative robot environments, focusing on safeguarding fellow agents within close proximity. We propose an integrated risk-aware control system that integrates the safety needs of the networked robots and their neighbors, and our method can adapt to various adversarial scenarios. We outline the key components of the framework, including the formulation of the safety issue, the development of a risk assessment model, and the design of a risk-informed control system. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework using a security-constrained navigation problem, and our method can successfully mitigate the safety needs of the robots and their surroundings.

Recent research has yielded new data for Andromeda XXV, a dwarf galaxy in the Andromeda galaxy's satellite cluster. Deep imaging studies conducted using the Hubble Space Telescope have allowed for the enhancement of the galaxy's radial profile down to 4 kiloparsecs from its core. The updated information has been used to assess the levels of dark matter and stellar content in Andromeda XXV. The findings from these studies support a two-component model consisting of stars and dark matter in the galaxy. The amount of dark matter present in Andromeda XXV has been found to be significantly lower than in other galaxies of a similar size. The research has also determined the mass of Andromeda XXV to be approximately 1.4 billion times the mass of the sun. In grant-free, massive IoT systems employing the multi-user detection technique, random, grant-free sequences are typically used to differentiate from one another. The sequences, being random, lack a specific property that their auto and cross-correlation values remain within a predetermined threshold. In contrast, non-orthogonal sequences, designed with a genetic algorithm tailored for IoT applications, are found to possess lower detection loss and achieve higher overall system performance. The genetic algorithm leverages the concept of multi-objective optimization to generate sequences with low detection loss and quantization noise, thereby yielding superior composite detection performance as compared to traditional, random sequences.

To develop accurate models of water in air, we must ensure that our models comply with thermodynamic principles. We have identified areas where existing models fall short and propose revised approaches that meet these criteria. Specifically, we address two widespread issues: the use of non-ideal equations in relation to non-ideal heat capacities and the application of linearized equations in relation to non-linear water vapor condensation. By rectifying these flaws, we have created more reliable models. We demonstrate the improvements through comparisons of approximate solutions as opposed to exact calculations.

We introduce two new types of algebraic structures within the framework of matroid theory, referred to as outer algebras. These structures are comprised of algebras that can be formed by combining a matroid with an outerform, a specific type of matrix-related structure. These outer forms are analogous to the dual of a matrix, but can be based on various subsets of matrix elements. The existence of these outer algebras generalizes concepts found in free and cyclic matroid theory, specifically the idea of "duality" that can be applied to both infinite and finite rank matroids. Additionally, we explore the relationship between algebraic properties in the context of these outer algebras.

Research has shown that accurate training of a dialogue state tracker is crucial for effective monitoring. However, existing ASR error checks have been conducted without considering the probability distributions of ASR output. This paper presents a method for calculating uncertainty in ASR output by utilizing the Word Confusion Networks framework, which is then applied to a dialogue state monitoring task. Our experiments indicate that incorporating the posterior distribution of ASR outputs in the calculation of dialogue state probabilities enhances the performance of a dialogue state monitor.

We demonstrate the existence of specific coherent sheaf structures on a complex algebraic curve, by numerically solving a system of linear equations using a central connection and a metric, which we define as the \emph{Calculus of Sheaves on a Curve (CSC)}.

The CSC method is applicable to any holomorphically fibre-bundle structure over a compact K\"ahler manifold with a relatively compact cone structure, including both projective and non-projective varieties.

By solving the CSC, we obtain explicit expressions for sheaves with given holomorphic sections, which generalizes existing results for abelian varieties and K3 surfaces, while revealing novel, previously unstudied properties.

Several prominent data structures, including stacks, queues, and graphs, serve as fundamental building blocks for numerous algorithms. A universal framework was developed to create these data structures using a basic set of operations. Despite the simplicity of this framework, its implementation in certain programming languages can be challenging due to limitations in their built-in data structures. Researchers have investigated the essential operations needed for implementing fundamental data structures in various programming languages, and the optimal set of operations for this purpose was identified. Notably, a programming language may require different minimal frameworks for evaluation and/or implementation. For example, Proc, a programming language with only recursion, can create stacks and queues using the following frameworks: Proc needs a single frame to implement a stack, but two queues require the use of pointers. In contrast, Proc can create graphs without any additional framework. Researchers have determined that Proc, a programming language with only recursion and environment shifting, cannot create queues without a framework. These findings highlight the importance of considering how operations are implemented in a programming language when evaluating its data structures.

Measuring entanglement in qubit systems, such as those found in optical systems, typically involves using the von Neumann entropy on the reduced density matrices of the quantum states. However, this conventional method is often impractical because it necessitates an accurate full density matrix, which is rarely known in many experiments. Instead, researchers often rely on classical correlations between specific measurements, such as those obtained from two detectors, to estimate entanglement. In this work, we introduce a novel approach for assessing entanglement using conventional linear optical systems and conventional measurements. Our method enables the precise determination of entanglement in two-qubit pure states and two-qubit mixed states by utilizing only the known reduced density matrix of one qubit. Furthermore, our approach is robust against errors in measurements and versatile in application, with potential use in various quantum information processing systems.

The data from the JET tokamak's eigenmode frequency database has been cross-referenced with the vascular characteristics of the trees surrounding the facility's site to identify a potential correlation. Observations indicate that an Edgerton-type high-speed camera captures palm tree oscillations with distinct periodicities (approximately 0.3 s, 0.6 s, 1.2 s, 2.4 s). Notably, the same frame rates yield images of the JET tokamak's plasma that exhibit oscillations in line positions during the last stationary phase of its discharges. Palm modes of lower frequency (about 29.5 Hz, 59 Hz, 119 Hz, 239 Hz) are detected in images, matching an underlying pattern of synchronized tree vibrations. Palm tree frequencies are found to align with a fundamental frequency of 239 Hz, closely matching a quarter of the 976.6 Hz frequency at which the JET vacuum vessel resonates. This suggests a possible connection to an acoustic phenomenon that arises when sound waves emitted by the vacuum chamber's excited modes induce synchronized tree vibrations.

Although significant advancements have been made in deep learning technologies, conventional machine learning techniques still perform effectively in continuous learning applications, with methods like using fixed network parameters or resetting part of the network, making them suitable alternatives. With the growing influence of transfer learning, utilizing a pre-trained model alongside a 'forgetful' network, such as an Adversarial Fine-tuning module, could further enhance performance. However, the widespread adoption of pre-trained models in continuous learning has led to a lack of basic method evaluation, with many sophisticated techniques building upon them. Our study investigates the applicability of pre-trained models in continuous learning and presents an uncomplicated method involving an 'Extended Random Initialisation' approach by merging weights from multiple training episodes. With comprehensive evaluation on multiple benchmarks, we reveal that our method surpasses or competes with more complex state-of-the-art techniques, with reduced computation and memory requirements. With this study, we aim to encourage the evaluation of simple methods and reduce reliance on the complex models that have dominated the field.

The rapid dissemination of social media content, including hate speech, has reached alarming levels, posing a threat to global society. Expertise in multiple languages is required to effectively manage the vast amount of available data, but a solution is not forthcoming. Our goal is to develop a hate speech classification system that is both efficient and easy to interpret on social media platforms, incorporating multiple types of data. To achieve this, we will refine existing advanced models by incorporating relevant linguistic features and modular explainability techniques. Our full system will analyze text and image simultaneously, allowing us to compare the performance of different modalities and provide transparent explanations for our model's decision-making process.

This paper examines the effects of degree distributions on networks of Type-I neurons, a specific type of neuronal model. We investigate how varying degree distributions in these networks influences their dynamic behavior. Building on existing research that utilized a specific degree distribution, we compare it to an alternative, more traditional log-normal distribution, while considering the effects of random perturbations. To quantify the differences in behavior between these networks, we calculate the average distance between neurons at different time points. Through numerical simulations, we evaluate their dynamic differences.

The repair of software faults has long been a difficult challenge for researchers and developers, who strive to minimize the repair of incorrect solutions. The second counter ablation strategy, introduced in this paper, presents an innovative repair approach counter to the conventional practice of utilizing unsupervised, randomly generated solutions. This method instead exploits conflicting patch generation, where the primary aim is to create repairs that are oppositively aligned in order to eliminate common flaws. The results of our experiments on the Bjorner repair corpus show that our proposed repair method achieves the best success rates across various metrics, particularly repair success, validity, and adherence to original code semantics.

The general identification-feasible identification capability region, or GIFC, is a mathematical concept used to assess the accuracy of parameter identification for dynamic systems. The identification capability region is comprised of all possible parameter vectors that can be identified given a dynamic system's model and corresponding data. The physical nature of data is characterized by a data spectrum, which is a categorization of data types such as noise, signal, and interference. This study introduces a novel approach to determining the GIFC for correlated data by distinguishing between signal-rich and signal-poor data regions. This data spectrum is used to develop an efficient and simplified method for calculating the GIFC. The proposed data spectrum based approach is more computationally cost-effective, and more intuitive than traditional methods making it a more preferred option.

The emergence of advanced and precise heavy-ion collision experiments has made it possible to acquire crucial insights into the properties of heavy nuclei. Specifically, it is now feasible to examine how fluid-like matter behaves under these conditions, which in turn allows us to make connections to the equation of state. While one- and two-particle observables provide valuable information on the system's fluid dynamics, they do not fully convey the complexity of collision structure. As a result, researchers are seeking more informative tools, which have led them to investigate time-dependent source structures using hydrodynamic models and Monte Carlo simulations. Our novel tool, known as the three-dimensional flow examination, has been developed to analyze the collision structure by comparing sources extracted from hydrodynamic models with those simulated using Monte Carlo methods on a event-by-event basis. This technique has been successfully implemented and tested using Monte Carlo simulations, which has also enabled the development of the first-ever map of the collision structure for specific experiments, such as the most peripheral Au+Au collisions in RHIC. Our tool has been made available to the public through public repositories, allowing for its shared use in the future.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to a significant increase in the need for rapid and precise disease diagnosis. Researchers have explored using portability of learning models from general to specific datasets. A common challenge in building disease prediction models is maintaining patient privacy, particularly when dealing with central databases. This study addresses two key issues: adversarial training to prevent data leakage when swapping models, and the privacy concerns associated with remote diagnosis. We employ a dual approach, using a disentanglement technique to isolate data variations and remove sensitive information, and a privacy protector to remove personal data features. An adversarial training mechanism is also used to prevent the model and adversarial training data from revealing the underlying data distribution. Our proposed method, HIP, is evaluated on real-world datasets through a comparison of its performance with the existing Fast-Net model. The results indicate that HIP not only maintains similar performance to Fast-Net but also demonstrates superior generalization capabilities and a significant reduction in data leakage.

Graph neural networks have demonstrated the ability to learn various real-world applications and have been successfully integrated into wireless communication systems for signal detection and channel estimation tasks. However, the current use of GNNs in wireless systems still faces limitations due to their centralized implementation, which restricts their scalability in large-scale systems. To address this issue, a recent study introduced a distributed GNN (DGNN) architecture for signal detection and channel estimation in multi-antenna systems, which can effectively handle data exchange and processing among nodes in large systems. In this paper, two DGNN models are developed for coherent and non-coherent detection, utilizing a message passing approach that can pass information between nodes in a graph. The results show that the DGNN architecture can offer superior performance compared to traditional methods, while its practical implementation in real-world systems depends on the limitations of wireless data transfer.

The trend in homicides in Goias, a large province in Brazil's Central West region, has been marked by a significant surge over the past two decades. Homicide rates in Goias have risen more than any other province in Brazil, with the exception of one, during this period. To gain insight into this disturbing trend, researchers employed statistical analysis to identify correlations and patterns in the data, which were then examined using a spatial clustering method. The results revealed significant links between a province's homicide rate and those of its neighbors, as well as temporal consistency in the data, with high rates persisting over the entire study period. The findings suggest that effective measures to combat high homicide rates in one area are likely to have a positive impact on neighboring provinces as well.

We aim to develop a stochastic gradient descent algorithm that can adapt to (i) varying learning rates based on sound intensity and (ii) accelerate convergence past a specific point. Existing research provides sound-adaptive techniques in (i), while problem transformation techniques in (ii) are well-known. However, there's a gap in developing a method that simultaneously achieves sound adaptation and accelerated convergence. This work combines techniques from Krawtchouk moments and an adaptive process to propose a novel algorithm, but it falls short of achieving accelerated convergence while relying on problematic transformation. To overcome this, we've developed a different approach, the Sound-adaptive Neural Network Algorithm, that utilizes sound intensity in (i) and has potential for further optimization in (ii). This method achieves sound adaptation through acoustic feature embedding and adaptive process adjustment. Additionally, it allows the incorporation of an extra neural network layer to analyze the gradient distribution and accelerate convergence in (ii). This approach outperforms existing methods in sound adaptation and has the potential to further improve convergence.

Axions emerge as a necessary solution to the strong CP problem and are further bolstered by their potential to additionally explain various aspects of the universe, such as baryogenesis and the missing dark matter. The axion haloscopes, particularly those in the microwave region, represent a highly promising approach for testing axion-like particle physics and gaining insight into the Sun's interior by searching for geoneutrino-related signatures. In this study, we explore the potential of the next-generation axion minitorque haloscope experiment, BabyIAXO, in utilizing the Sun as a massive target to detect axions or, conversely, infer information about the Sun's interior by measuring its nucleus-related X-ray emission. We find that, with improvements in BabyIAXO's sensitivity, this experiment may be able to identify evidence of nuclear transitions within the Sun, thus complementing existing geoneutrino searches and solar interior studies.

A class of non-synchronized oscillating systems is identified, characterized by a unique trigger point where excitement builds into a loop, when the system ceases to be excited. It's observed that this unique trigger point can either expand or contract depending on the system parameters. It's also shown that standardized equations for this category of systems can be derived from their original form. As a case study, this concept is applied to simple penduluses acted upon by magnetic or gravitational forces with an amplitude modulation, revealing the derivation process and identification of the standardized equation's trigger point.

Highly advanced robotic arms are equipped with multiple mechanical fingers that allow them to be classified as dexterous robotic hands. These hands have been successfully used in various industrial settings to enhance productivity and carry out intricate tasks. Despite the significant progress made in developing robotic hands, the lack of a comprehensive grasp database has hindered their full potential from being utilized in more complex tasks such as research in simulation environments. Consequently, the application of these robotic hands in real-world tasks outside of their original manufacturing settings has been limited. In an attempt to address this issue, a simulated collection of robotic grasps called DexGraspNet has been developed. This collection, comprising over 2.5 million grasps of over 12,000 objects, is expected to provide a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners to employ in their work. The full scope and implementation details of DexGraspNet have been documented online for the purpose of promoting collaborative research.

A novel turbo spin-echo sequence for T2-weighted imaging has been developed and utilizes multiple breath-holds without any requirement for patient restraint, while providing compensation for respiratory variations to ensure comprehensive scanning. The sequence employs four-dimensional imaging, combining three-dimensional spatial data with respiratory phase information, to provide extensive coverage of the anatomy. To facilitate reproducible imaging, patients are positioned in an optimized manner to maintain consistent respiratory patterns throughout the scanning process. To acquire high-quality T2-weighted images in four dimensions, patients execute a series of repeated deep inspirations during the scanning procedure. To account for the dynamic effects of respiratory movement on the image, an advanced technique incorporating spatial-shift-encoding data is utilized to generate additional contrast, thus enhancing visibility of the image. To our knowledge, this approach represents the first use of a turbo spin-echo sequence for four-dimensional imaging. To validate the effectiveness of the sequence, comprehensive body scans were performed on ten patients, resulting in large datasets of over 500 three-dimensional images. To evaluate the accuracy of the sequence, a quantitative assessment was conducted, demonstrating that motion correction provided improved image clarity and contrast, particularly for structures in close proximity to the respiratory diaphragm. The novel sequence offers a significant advancement in turbo spin-echo imaging, providing superior image quality and contrast, particularly for structures in close proximity to the diaphragm.

We introduce InDistill, a novel model compression technique, which accurately preserves data flows in both the teacher and student models to yield superior performance. We distinguish ourselves from conventional knowledge distillation approaches by incorporating continuous post-processing. Notably, InDistill achieves notable improvements over existing methods. We implement the method using multiple model architectures, incorporating pre-trained teachers with or without supervision, as well as a unified framework for compressing models. We achieve significant performance enhancements in terms of accuracy versus FLOPs ratio. The method is comprehensive, adaptable to any teacher-student model pair, and is effectively used to compress pre-trained models. We achieve notable improvements in image classification models and model compression of transformer-based language models, which often employ knowledge distillation to overcome the challenges of model compression in sequence-to-sequence tasks.

Two compact metric spaces, M and N, are topologically similar if there's a homeomorphism mapping points to points. This note explores the connection between the topological similarity of a linear-like submersion function on a plane and that of its associated foliation. Given a set of real numbers, (α, β, γ, δ), such that α ≠ 0, we demonstrate that linear-like submersion functions on a plane with parameters (α, β, γ, δ) are topologically equivalent if and only if their associated foliations are also topologically equivalent.

The effects of intermittent non-resident grazing on dry-land plant species are still not fully understood. In this study, we have explored the impact of periodic grazing on an ecosystem where herbivores only consume available vegetation when present. Our findings suggest that transient non-resident grazing can lead to a state of equilibrium where vegetation and grazing coexist, unlike resident grazing which typically results in the disappearance of either or both species. Notably, brief periods of grazing while grazing species are abundant can induce the emergence of grazing-free equilibrium. These outcomes vary significantly based on grazing duration and frequency.

In recent years, researchers have discovered that the same techniques used for dimensionality reduction, such as Linear Sketching, can provide effective solutions for a variety of challenging computational problems across theoretical and practical domains. Focusing on the CountSketch method, this study aims to explore the resilience of this dimensionality reduction technique when dealing with adversarially altered data. Specifically, the research investigates the limits of its applicability in the context of various computational tasks, including estimating frequencies, matrix norms, and semi-definite programming problems. Crucially, the work identifies key distinctions between computational tasks in terms of how effectively CountSketch withstands adversarial tampering.

Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) is an established computational method offering precise ground states, especially useful for molecules.  Its effectiveness can be enhanced through the incorporation of variational influence function theory (VIF) corrections.  This study introduces ipie, a flexible Python-based QMC code that executes efficiently across CPUs and GPUs.  ipie utilizes VIF, has integrated lattice transformations, and supports various fermion and cluster algorithms.  To validate its performance, ipie is tested on VIF-corrected systems, including the t-J model with up to 8 sites on a 2D cluster and the bilayer hybrid layer cuprate model at specific values.  These results are then compared to results from VMC and other QMC packages.

To establish a secure high-speed trading platform on the Quantum Cloud, a trusted partnership is necessary for client-server communication. A proposed system incorporates quantum key distribution for secure data transfer, coupled with advanced encryption protocols from SSL/TLS. This hybrid approach enables the creation of a secure environment for quantum key distribution and key verification, protecting client data on the Quantum Cloud. A comprehensive security evaluation was conducted to develop a reliable and efficient high-speed trading platform.

A market where brokers exist, consisting of buyers, brokers, sellers, and items, is investigated. The perfect brokerage system optimizes the quantity of brokers based on the number of transactions, while a suboptimal system generates revenue for brokers through a specified formula. The focus is on finding the maximum revenue achievable by brokers in the suboptimal system and analyzing how revenue and the number of transactions correlate. Additionally, strategies employed by brokers and their effects on the market outcome are examined, along with the identification of a unique market state responsible for revenue generation.

To facilitate reading comprehension, abstractive summarization models are often fine-tuned to generate more informative summaries. However, current techniques typically rely on pre-defined command prompts that are limited in their ability to adapt to diverse situations. To overcome this challenge, researchers have proposed using pre-trained language models as factorized decision makers to issue instance-specific commands during inference. In this paper, we introduce an alternative approach that involves training a model to generate abstractive summaries using entity-specific prompts acquired through planning. Our approach can discover relevant entities and construct a prompt that leads to an effective summary in an iterative process. Our experiments show that this method can successfully identify essential entities and create a prompt that yields a better summary in most cases. Our findings also suggest that our approach can generalize to unseen data and produce high-quality summaries in approximately half the length of the original text while maintaining similar fidelity.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiability of a given $n$-dimensional function, based on the differentiability of a related $(n-1)$-dimensional function, while exploring the relationship between these conditions and existing theorems in the field.

Research has established a link between emotional authenticity in speech and the listener's ability to synchronize with the speaker's vocal patterns. This study aims to identify and quantify instances where speakers adapt their vocal rhythms in response to others through an in-depth analysis of raw speech signals. A custom algorithm is developed to measure vocal coordination in conversational interactions, focusing on the intrinsic characteristics of speech production. To assess its effectiveness, the algorithm is tested on a controlled dataset comparing human-human conversations with computer-generated voices and recorded human voices. A strong correlation is found between the algorithm's output and human judgments of vocal synchrony, demonstrating its validity. Furthermore, the research reveals that speakers tend to synchronize their vocal rhythms more readily when the intervals between their words are longer, indicating a relationship between vocal coordination and the inherent patterns of speech pauses and linkages.

A modified version of the Martin-Sollerman theory has been developed for categorizing quantum manipulations that work within an arbitrary Hilbert space structure for both pure and mixed states. It specifically builds upon the Martin-Sollerman theory by replacing the unitary group with the unitary sphere, SU(d+1), to create a new version, Lambda-S1. This expansion, Lambda-S1, accommodates quantum manipulations that have dimensional restrictions, such as those involving quantum entanglement and non-conserving projective measurements. Categorical models for pure and mixed states have been established within Lambda-S1, demonstrating its applicability in understanding quantum systems with restricted dimensional properties.

Analytical calculations have been conducted for two types of quasiparticle excitations, specifically the quasiparticle and quasihole, in the fractional quantum Hall effect, with a focus on energy and charge density. Calculations were based on the composite fermion theory, resulting in analytical solutions for energy and charge density profils, validated through comparison with Monte Carlo simulations and experimental energy measurements. Analytical solutions were achieved by employing the variational approach, yielding precise quantitative results. Furthermore, this research has enabled the analysis of electron density between a quasiparticle and quasihole, demonstrating a dip in charge density profile.

In the context of glaciology, particularly when modeling contact problems involving marine ice sheets, a semicoercive variational Stokes inequality arises. This study explores the convergence rates of the finite element error in both the continuous and discrete galcial contact problems, with the analysis extended to account for stress Jacobi preconditioning.

High-mass star formation is a major driver of galactic-scale outflows, which in turn can limit star formation efficiency. Using observations from KCWI, we studied how these outflows regulate star formation in a dwarf galaxy that is actively producing stars. Our analysis of a bursting galaxy at redshift z=0.4 reveals how these outflows modulate the star-formation rate based on the galaxy's inclination. In this study, we examine the impact of outflows on 6 nearby galaxies, of mass similar to the Milky Mercury-like galaxies, using KCWI observations. Our analysis of H-alpha maps reveals that outflows have the capacity to suppress star formation via outflow-driven feedback. This effect is particularly pronounced in edge-on galaxies, where outflows lead to reduced star formation. Our findings from DUVET's sample of rapidly star-forming galaxies support the notion that outflows serve as a mechanism to control star formation via the blocking of gas inflow through the production of a thick disk. This process is a common mechanism to limit star formation in disk galaxies. This effect is particularly pronounced in disk galaxies, of mass similar to the Milky Mercury-like galaxies, which have outflows that are able to block the flow of gas to their centers. This mechanism is a common means of limiting star formation in disk galaxies.

In this study, researchers examined triangular flow in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at various energies using a multiphase transport model. They found that the Au+Au collisions displayed significant triangular flow, which decreased slightly as energy increased. The triangular flow signal in Cu+Cu collisions was much weaker, and tended to rise with energy. The study also found that initial state geometry played a major role in developing triangular flow. By comparing simulations to existing data, researchers determined that the transport model accurately captured triangular flow's dependence on collision centrality and energy level.

This study introduces a novel robotic structure called Simultaneous Robotic Structure (SRS), featuring a modular and distributed design to enhance collaborative and efficient working habits in workplaces characterised by adverse environmental conditions. The robotic network is designed to withstand harsh situations, even when individual modules fail. The distributed architecture allows for the achievement of desired shapes and structures through continuous and flexible material arrangement. We examine various robotic configurations, such as meshes, surfaces, and networks, to identify the most effective models for withstanding external forces. Experimental tests using 3D-printed prototypes have proven that the proposed robotic structure can maintain stability in harsh environments, even after module failure. The SRS's adaptability and durability make it suitable for challenging robotic applications. A video demonstrating the experiment can be found at https://youtu.be/6Q9Q9Q9Q9Q.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation in images requires extensive computation and often involves using vast datasets to achieve satisfactory results. To minimize costs associated with such processes, researchers explore alternative methods of pre-training their networks using simpler tasks before applying them to more complex problems. Conventional wisdom suggests that classification tasks are the most suitable starting point for this approach; however, recent studies have shown that using monocular depth estimation for pre-training can lead to better results. We demonstrate that using depth estimation for pre-training is beneficial due to two key factors. Firstly, depth and semantic labeling exhibit spatial correlations, which enable seamless transfer of task-related information. Secondly, depth prediction involves both scalar and spatial variations, which allow for the distribution of task-related information across different spatial scales. We experimentally validate the effectiveness of this approach and show that using depth estimation for pre-training can produce more efficient results than using traditional color-based classification approaches.

Let's consider the set of all mappings that are log-harmonic and starlike, defined within the unit disk in the complex plane. In this context, we establish the maximum possible value of the Bohr radius for mappings that satisfy certain conditions, including log-harmonic starlikeness with either normal or subnormal coefficients. Our investigation builds upon existing research related to log-harmonic mappings, while employing a novel approach that leverages the properties of convex functions to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying mathematics.

We have developed methods to estimate Kendall's tau nonparametric rank correlation coefficient and its associated variance. The proposed test is a modification of the Hoeffding test, offering improved performance through better approximation of the null chi-squared distribution and more efficient computation. The new methods are specifically designed to be more effective, particularly for smaller sample sizes, while maintaining the same test power for larger samples. The suggested methods are particularly beneficial for smaller samples, outperforming the Hoeffding test, which was the previous best available option. The methods work well in a simulated scenario where sample tau values are estimated, and in another where the test is performed on real data. The methods hold significant value in a real-world scenario where the test is performed on real data.

As edge intelligence gains momentum in the automotive world, concerns about protecting users' data privacy in vehicular networks are mounting, prompting calls for comprehensive solutions. This study addresses these concerns by presenting a unified framework for privacy preservation in edge computing systems, emphasizing robust data security and protecting users' sensitive information. This framework, tailored to non-secure plies, leverages advanced techniques like attribute-based encryption and provable security methods to ensure rigorous data security. Additionally, we incorporate fuzzy-based protocols to safeguard users' data from unauthorized exposure. This framework's efficacy is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and verification, using real-world traffic data to showcase its practical relevance and value. This study provides a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners to develop privacy-enhancing solutions in edge computing systems, with applications in vehicular networks.

A new set of topological surfaces, known as the Euler topological surfaces, are introduced and defined by specific values of n for the 2-dimensional surface SG(n). The study of these surfaces reveals that SG(n) exists for odd n values greater than 2. The characteristics of these surfaces are explored through the application of an extended version of the Euler-Poincar\'e formula, along with the computation of their homotopy groups via a specific set of loops. Additionally, the relationships between the surface SG(n) are analyzed for selected values of n, including n = 3, 5, and 7. The study also delves into the properties of their universal cover and the corresponding fundamental group of these surfaces. A thorough examination of the surface properties is provided through the representation of the fundamental group in a specific mathematical format. The research further involves the computation of the k-th homotopy group for loop-based systems on the surface SG(n). A thorough theoretical analysis of the surface properties is provided in relation to their generalizations, and the findings are compared with existing research in the field.

The Holling-Tanner predator-prey model has been revised to incorporate a unique nonlinearity in prey growth, driven by an Allee effect, which affects population growth below a specific threshold. This modification aligns with real-world population dynamics, as growth is generally impaired when populations drop below a certain minimum. By examining the model's behavior, particularly in regions where the Allee effect is pronounced, it was found that population recovery from low levels can be swift, yet vulnerable to extinction, especially when populations fall below a critical critical threshold for an extended period. This vulnerability stems from a singular, unstable equilibrium point near the Allee threshold, which can be exploited by predator-prey cycles, further increasing extinction risk. This theoretical work lays the foundation for exploring the model's behavior in diverse contexts, from theoretical to real-world applications.

This article presents a comprehensive analysis of the initial results from a groundbreaking approach known as Aspect Pivot, a method for updating an approximate simplex table in linear programming. This update technique generates a sequence of feasible points by progressively moving, in a deterministic manner, away from the ordinary pivot choices made in standard simplex method iterations. Our findings confirm that the convergence rate of the Aspect Pivot method is linear under all unfavorable conditions, while also highlighting scenarios where it outperforms traditional methods. A distinctive feature of the approach lies in the construction of "deterministic" directions of unbounded iterations. A technical report previously published in 2017 had already predicted a linear convergence rate under unfavorable circumstances; this current work serves as a rigorous proof and analysis. A subsequent article will explore the application of the method in a completely deterministic setting.
This study aims to extend Nikodym kernels to modular lattices, examining their relationship with graded rings and generalized boolean algebras in the process.

This paper examines the top quark mass extraction in the presence of top quark productions with additional jets, focusing on the influence of off-shell contributions. Partial phase space cuts are applied to ttbar events to distinguish them from the background based on the number of jets, hadronic transverse momentum, and the transverse energy of the jets. Two different collider energies are considered: the LHC at 7 and 14 TeV. Mass resolutions are calculated for the ttbar systemreconstructing the top quark mass from the transverse momentum of the top quark, which is calculated using neural networks, at both energies. The effect of partial phase space cuts on the mass extraction is also investigated. The results show that off-shell contributions have a significant impact on the mass extraction, particularly at the LHC at 7 TeV, where the difference in the mass resolution with and without off-shell contributions is around 20%. The effect of partial phase space cuts on the mass resolution is also significant, ranging from 20% to 40%. The study at the LHC at 14 TeV shows that the influence of off-shell contributions on the mass extraction is smaller, with a difference in the mass resolution with and without off-shell contributions of around 8%. The effect of partial phase space cuts on the mass resolution is also significant, ranging from 25% to 50%.

Recent advancements in Zero-shot facial imitation tasks have been primarily driven by the widespread adoption of Transformers and pre-trained models such as FaceX-ray and Disentangled Face Representation (DFR). Previous research has focused on evaluating the effectiveness of architectures like ResNets and Xception, but a new study reveals that Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures can significantly outperform these established methods. Building upon this finding, the study introduces the FaZeViT model, a highly accurate solution for zero-shot counterfeit detection that has been validated on two benchmark datasets, UCR and CSU, and has outperformed the state-of-the-art approach by achieving an impressive 3.3% improvement in classification accuracy. By conducting an in-depth analysis of ViT architecture, the study also identifies the key factors contributing to its success and provides valuable insights for further research in Zero-shot counterfeit detection.

A significant challenge in the field of artificial intelligence is creating a sophisticated, intelligent agent that can navigate complex environments. In the context of a self-driving vehicle, the agent must utilize available data to interpret its surroundings, including fellow entities, and make informed decisions within a multi-dimensional system. In this research paper, the concepts of Deep Reinforcement Learning and autonomous vehicles are discussed, and a basic model for a self-driving vehicle has been proposed, which takes into account the multiple layers of data collection and processing in these systems. Additionally, the potential shortcomings of existing Deep Reinforcement Learning models as potential solutions for these complexities, and possible approaches to mitigating them through the use of latent variables, are explored.

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements in efficiently solving complex multi-objective optimization problems. A popular parallelization technique known as parallel evolutionary algorithms can effectively solve high-dimensional problems by utilizing multiple candidate solutions in parallel. However, the asynchronous execution of evaluations can lead to an uneven distribution of computational time among the candidate solutions, resulting in slower progression of infeasible individuals and biased selection processes. This phenomenon, referred to as Evaluation Time Bias, can greatly impact the performance of parallel evolutionary algorithms. To address this issue, a novel parent selection technique is proposed that mitigates the effects of Evaluation Time Bias by incorporating frequency data into the selection process. The proposed approach is then evaluated on three multi-dimensional test functions, followed by a comparative analysis with existing bias-reducing methods. The results demonstrate that the proposed technique is more efficient than existing methods and effectively addresses Evaluation Time Bias.

Recent analysis of the 2017 gravitational microlensing event OGLE-2017-BLG-1434 has yielded a detailed set of data, revealing an exoplanet with mass similar to that of Neptune and an orbital path that is highly elliptical in nature. The planet, designated OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, has a temperature that is extremely low, approximately 50 Kelvin. Utilizing the Keck Observatory's adaptive optics system, the researchers were able to verify the planet's presence and collect data on its orbital characteristics, including the distance from the observer (3.0 kiloparsecs) and mass (0.075 solar masses), as well as its distance from the host star (1.25 astronomical units) and orbital period (82.45 years). The analysis also confirmed the host star's mass (0.29 solar masses) and the entire system's mass (0.77 solar masses). Due to its proximity to the observer, the planet's light can potentially be directly observed in the near future, making OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb a significant discovery in the field of astronomy and astrophysics.

The time-oscillating Lindblad generator holds significant importance in the quantum theory of light. It has been pivotal in the creation of time-domain soliton models, which have contributed substantially to the understanding of nonlinear light field dynamics. Specifically, the concept has been applied in the context of Kerr compressors and Kerr solitons in both linear and nonlinear light systems. This paper will present an approximation technique known as high-rate expansions, which enables the transformation of the time-oscillating Lindblad generator at high propagation rates into a diffusion-type operator. This approximation technique holds similarities with other approximate methods such as the Wigner distribution and the Monte-Carlo method, which will also be discussed in detail.

The presence of a long-range ferromagnetic order in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ with $0.15<x<0.25$ affects the way neutrons get polarized as they scatter with the magnetic order. This effect, seen in neutron spin polarization (NSP) in the course of a time-dependent process, is studied using the zero-field muon spin relaxation ($\mu$SR) method. The data suggests that the material undergoes a phase transition from a long-range ferromagnetic order to an antiferromagnetic or spin glass state as $x$ increases, with the first transition happening at $x\sim0.20$. The nature of the spin glass state is further investigated by analyzing the equilibrium NSP in the course of a temperature-dependent process. The material CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ with $0.20<x<0.25$ displays a temperature-dependent equilibrium NSP that is characteristic of a Ginzburg-Landau type of spin glass for the charge and magnetic properties, with the magnetic properties being affected more by the variation in $x$.

The formation of massive stars impacts their surroundings with intense radiation and strong outflows, creating conditions that can give rise to massive star-forming regions, known as cometary globules. These areas, identified in the star-forming region G176.51+00.20 through the ASKAP telescope, are found to be associated with a large-scale ionized structure. Observations of the 21-cm line toward CG G176.51+00.20, using the ASKAP and ATCA telescopes, have uncovered significant self-absorption, indicating the presence of warm and cold components in the interstellar medium. These components are found to be aligned with the radiation beam, particularly in the line-of-sight toward the massive star-forming region where a cometary globule resides. The measured line-of-sight velocity suggests that the star system G176.51+00.20 is located at a distance of approximately 4.4 kpc. Velocities measured in the 21-cm line mapping, using the ASKAP telescope, show that the star system G176.51+00.20 is rotating in a clockwise direction.

We introduce new definitions for intermediate and avaricious versions of beta shifts, with the latter characterised by the absence of certain types of factors. By examining beta shifts with a single irrational transfer function coefficient, we demonstrate the existence of intervals in the beta parameter space where intermediate and avaricious versions differ, while also establishing conditions under certain beta values with periodic or aperiodic dynamics.

Determining the CP angle phi s resulting from the CP violation in the quark system involves measuring differences between decay modes involving mesons with specific CP properties. In this study, we investigated the decay of B_s mesons into J/psi particles accompanied by two pi atoms, focusing on the ratio of four pi systems' yields to those of two pi systems, as well as the difference between their strong phase shifts, to directly extract phi s. Our findings, based on 7.4 fb-1 of integrated luminosity recorded at the LHCb experiment, are consistent with standard model predictions.

Deep neural networks are notoriously reliant on data from their initial training environment. However, there's an emerging trend of transferring them to other domains for image recognition tasks. Our research delves into the various methods employed for DNN domain transfer, focusing on image classification and retrieval. Assessing a wide range of techniques, including adaptive training, domain adaptation, and generative models, our analysis provides an in-depth review of the current state of DNN domain transfer. We also evaluate the effectiveness of 24 prominent deep learning datasets, providing comprehensive insights that can inform the development of new methods for DNN domain transfer.

Consider the projective space $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_q)$, and for a fixed $k \leq q$, count the number of ordered $k$-tuples of non-degenerate segments in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$ that intersect at most when $3\Delta(k+1)$ terms, where $\Delta$ denotes the greatest integer divisor. This count is equivalent to a $\mathbb{F}_q$-enriched version of a combinatorial problem first identified by J. Kahn in 2013, with implications for a longstanding conjecture in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$ and a recent proposal by P. Ruzsa.

In a regular triangular lattice, certain adjacent triangles are mutually exclusive.
This exclusion demonstrates a "law of triangular exclusion," which cannot be inferred from basic principles of geometry.
The only justification for this law is the assumption that it is inherent in the structure of the triangular lattice.
This contradiction highlights a limitation in proofs that rely solely on geometry and implies that some truths in geometry may be unsupported assertions.

Graph Neural Networks are now a leading choice for processing intricate graph-structured data, offering improved accuracy compared to conventional deep learning models. Despite their success, creating and training GNN models can be a daunting task, especially for users who lack expertise in deep learning. To address this issue, we developed a pioneering interpreter for GNN models, which can estimate model parameters with remarkable accuracy using a substantial dataset. This interpreter can also identify the most influential graph attributes for a specific model. Unlike existing research, our approach allows scaling up to larger and more complex models, which was previously a major limitation. We have successfully applied our interpreter to models of varying complexity, achieving results as high as 96.41% accuracy in node classification and 100% accuracy in link prediction.

The peculiar galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 was studied by analyzing its X-ray emission structure. This analysis involved examining the intensity distribution, spatial cluster substructures, and temperature variations. The study revealed the presence of a primary X-ray emission core, as well as two smaller clusters, denoted as A and B, located at distances of 360 and 540 kpc from the central core. Temperature readings of 3.53 and 3.80 keV were obtained for A and B, respectively. Notably, the X-ray emission appeared offset by approximately 10-15 arcseconds in the direction of cluster substructure A, suggesting that cluster A is pointing towards the central core.

The recently-proposed Legendre Memory Module (LMM) commences training with arbitrary initial values, and throughout the process gradually refines its kernel matrices, which are multi-dimensional parallelizable. As a result, the LMM can be efficiently trained in parallel on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, allowing for substantial time savings. This research demonstrates that models of the same type, but with varying initial states, converge to similar states. Furthermore, the study identifies the specific conditions under which this convergence occurs. Based on these findings, a new training method is developed, which differs from the standard backpropagation approach. This alternative method can be employed with models of the same type, and is likely to result in similar final model performances when used as a pre-training technique. This method also has the potential to be used as a regular training approach for more specialized models. This research also introduces a new performance metric to gauge the accuracy of LMM models, and provides a comprehensive comparison of different training approaches, including a discussion of potential future research directions.

As we approach the tenth anniversary of the initial Higgs boson discovery, which marked the end of a decades-long search, we now find ourselves engaged in a new quest to uncover additional weakly-interacting particles. A heightened sense of excitement prevails, driven by the emergence of anomalies in existing particle physics data that may point to the presence of new particles, as well as by the potential of cutting-edge technologies in experiments and particle collision studies at larger scales.

We're examining the development of a simulated naming system among a group of individuals, with each agent residing in a 2D space where they interact with neighboring agents to create language consistency. As a starting point, each agent possesses a unique word, and interactions with neighbors involve exchanging words in an attempt to create commonality. We've analyzed the effect of agent movement and their updated approach on developing consistent naming conventions within the community.

A lot of research has focused on spectrally-filtered PINNs, which add noise to the residual, hoping to balance bias and variance in these models. By using a residual with added noise, PDE-solutions derived from noisy data are more expressive, which is similar to using a smoother filter. We found that using a residual with noise is sufficient to overcome the spectral bias issue in PINNs, eliminating the need for additional spectral filters. We also discovered that using a gradient-based optimization technique in PINNs can reduce the impact of spectral bias, which is similar to the effect of noise in the residual. Finally, we proposed an approach to visualize and quantify the effects of spectral bias on PINN training and prediction loss surfaces using t-SNE. Our analysis revealed that using a gradient-based optimizer, such as Adam, can reduce spectral bias more effectively than adding noise to the residual, which is surprising since momentum can exponentially amplify gradient updates, potentially increasing the impact of spectral bias. Our study provides a more complete understanding of the effects of spectral bias in PINNs and how to mitigate them.

We examine three-dimensional linear Kelvin-Voigt beams over a bounded area to illustrate how energy decay is influenced by timing differences in elastic and viscoelastic waves within the material. By perturbing the viscoelastic parameter in the Bessel function $j_{\nu_1}(\sqrt{\lambda_i} x)$, we create localized modifications to the decay rate. By assuming that the perturbations remain small, we demonstrate that the affected modes continue to decay at a rate determined by the disturbed wavenumber, while the remaining modes remain stable indefinitely. This study extends previous research on waves in Kelvin-Voigt materials, providing new insights into the behavior of linked waves in these materials.

In the realm of games and robotic learning, explainable reinforcement learning holds significant importance due to its potential to extract usable rules from complex decision-making processes, which can be applied across various related tasks. Our research focuses on developing an XRL system that utilizes Inductive Logic Programming, allowing the generation of abstract and general rules from observed experiences. This XRL model is built upon a high-level abstract action space, enabling the detection and identification of underlying patterns in rewards. With its ability to extract perceivable rules, our XRL system is capable of solving challenging multi-object manipulation learning problems more efficiently than comparative models.

We've demonstrated a phenomenon where quantum compression leads to the loss of optical coherence in the system. The research reveals that certain nonlinear optical properties emerge as a result of the interaction between thermal processes and quantum compression, ultimately giving rise to irreversible optical behavior within the system. The study also shows that even in the absence of mechanical losses, the direction of propagation can be irreversibly altered due to the phenomenon of quantum compression. The findings suggest that quantum compression offers a novel method for producing and manipulating nonreversible optical effects. Furthermore, the research highlights the potential benefits of combining quantum compression with existing thermal methods to explore and investigate these nonreversible phenomena.

This research paper investigates a specific type of mathematical problem known as a Fenton type minimax challenge, in which the goal is to determine the magnitude of the largest possible difference between two types of summations: the sum of translates of a given function and the sum of the function itself, both evaluated over a specific interval. Previous studies by Fenton have focused on understanding the largest possible differences between these types of summations for functions with certain characteristics on the integer line, while our work extends this by analyzing the same problem for functions that can be translated. We derive mathematical expressions for the optimal configurations and provide bounds on the magnitudes of these differences. Furthermore, our study also identifies the critical roles played by Fourier series and Gibbs phenomena.

The CRESST II experiment is equipped to analyze Li-based crystals that can detect low-energy nuclear interactions with a high level of sensitivity. By analyzing the reduced-mass nuclear recoil energy and the reduced-mass kinetic energy of the crystals, direct limits can be placed on interactions involving spin, as studied with $^{6}$Li. Using the historical data from CRESST II, interactions involving a proton and neutron at the same time, known as spin-dependent interactions, can be studied. By assuming that dark matter particles interact with the proton and neutron in the same way, known as assumptions, the experiment has found new restrictions on such interactions, specifically with a mass less than 1 TeV. These restrictions were particularly stringent, with a mass fraction of the Earth's material being able to bind together as low as $5\times10^{-5}~$eV. By analyzing the data from CRESST II, the experiment has found new restrictions on such interactions, specifically with a mass less than 1 TeV. The goal of kernel mixture is investigated to model the non-Gaussian residual error term in blind image restoration. At its core, a kernel mixture is a blend of Gaussian distributions, each representing a distinct probability measure. By extending Horsfield's work, it is demonstrated that any probability measure can be approximated by a Gaussian probability measure. Consequently, it is possible to achieve a Gaussian mixture that accurately represents any probability measure. Building on this concept, we propose a novel approach to blind image restoration, where the non-Gaussian residual error term is modeled using a Gaussian mixture. To validate the effectiveness of our method, we employ a numerical algorithm to solve the conjugate primal-dual feasible solution space and apply it to various image restoration tasks.

This work introduces a new concept called associative Yang-Baxter algebras that go beyond uniformity, allowing for the generalization of uniform, left and right associative Yang-Baxter algebras. From this extension, we derive categories of right and left modules, examine coalgebra properties, and define equivalent concepts to bihom and cohom algebras. A notable example of a non-uniform associative Yang-Baxter algebra arises from the study of finite abelian groups of order n. Moreover, we establish a connection between these algebras and triangular R-matrices associated with finite symmetric associations under specific conditions.

Hoare Logic provides a solid foundation for formally verifying how programs transform input data into output data via well-defined input-output relationships. However, when dealing with complex, real-world programs and specifications involving intricate data relationships, authors face significant hurdles in crafting precise formal statements. To address this challenge, this research introduces a new method of verifying how programs modify input data to comply with the requirements outlined in input-output relationships. This approach, called Natural Hoare Reasoning, automates the process of verifying imperative programs based on natural language statements, utilizing a natural language parser and an analysis tool to determine semantic meaning. Our method is an extension of traditional Hoare Logic verification, incorporating natural language specifications for greater clarity and ease of use. By comparing the effectiveness of Natural Hoare Reasoning and traditional methods, authors conducted practical verifications of programs written in both C and Python, demonstrating improved usability and verifiability.

Distributed consensus is a vital task for numerous applications by having multiple entities agree on a single data item or state. Due to the potential for failures and malicious behavior, advanced consensus protocols have been developed. We are introducing RCanopus, a novel consensus protocol built on top of canopus, an existing state-of-the-art protocol. RCanopus is specifically designed with high failure resilience and resistance to malicious interventions in mind. It achieves exceptional performance by only requiring the use of three network hops from any given node. Furthermore, our comprehensive evaluation of RCanopus involves assessing it under diverse scenarios of failures and malicious behavior, testing it against various consensus metrics, and including a real-world implementation of the protocol.

We examine how the presence of cholesterol affects the bending resistance of lipid membranes using a simplified model that represents the energy cost of membrane deformations, quantified in terms of the in-plane and out-of-plane strain components. Our approach is rooted in the concept that this cost is directly linked to the energy per area of the membrane. Cholesterol's influence is represented by an adjustable parameter, known as the Lammertink parameter, which we calculate based on the energy difference between bilayer and micelle configurations of the cholesterol molecule. Our results reveal that the Lammertink parameter has a relatively low value of approximately 0.65, indicating a moderate level of constraint in the cholesterol molecule and relatively small energy losses when it is incorporated into lipid membranes. We further demonstrate that the presence of cholesterol leads to a decrease in the bending modulus of the membrane, causing the transition temperature to lower absolute values and broader distributions of the in-plane and out-of-plane strain components. These findings are consistent with experimental and simulation data, offering a straightforward method to determine the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid membranes.

The investigation into stellar cores focuses on the behavior of matter under extreme conditions, and a model developed based on the Arrovitz-Misner Hamiltonian reveals a remarkable similarity between loop quantum gravity and the self-similar pattern observed in these cores. This similarity gives rise to a new theoretical framework known as the loop quantum astrophysical model (LQAM). In this study, we explore the implications of LQAM on the physical properties of these cores, and provide a mathematical explanation for their self-similar pattern by analyzing a non-linear differential equation that governs the dynamics of LQAM.

This comprehensive list includes events examined in a preceding study, augmented by an additional 28 events examined in a subsequent investigation. The events in the catalog can be accessed online through the link indicated below, where corresponding figures and raw data are also provided.
